title: Complete Lattices
quickIdea: A complete lattice has a join and a meet for every subset, not just every pair. Every finite lattice is complete, and every complete lattice is bounded.
remember: A lattice is complete when every subset - including the empty set and the whole set - has a LUB and a GLB in the lattice.
Every finite lattice is complete: joins and meets of finite subsets are built pair by pair, and the empty subset has the least and greatest elements as its bounds.
Every complete lattice is bounded: the join of the empty set is the least element and its meet is the greatest element.
The converse fails: the set of rationals under the usual order has no greatest element, so the join of the whole set does not exist and the poset is not complete.
A subset lattice (a family of sets closed under union and intersection) is a lattice of sets, and it is complete exactly when it is closed under arbitrary unions and intersections.
GATE CSE 2004 Q.73 is the canonical completeness question: with S = {{1,2}, {1,2,3}, {1,3,5}, {1,2,4}, {1,2,3,4,5}} under set containment, adding {1} alone makes the family complete.

Why {1} suffices: for the pair {1,2,3} and {1,3,5} no member of S is contained in both, so the pair has no meet; once {1} is added it becomes the meet of that pair, and {1} is likewise the meet of {1,3,5} and {1,2,4}. Adding {1} also gives the family a least element, since {1} is contained in every member.

example.prompt: For S = {{1,2}, {1,2,3}, {1,3,5}, {1,2,4}, {1,2,3,4,5}} under containment, find a subset with no greatest lower bound, and the smallest set to add.
example.work: The meet of a family is its intersection when that intersection is a member of S. The pair {1,2,3} and {1,3,5}: no member of S is contained in both, so there is no meet. The pair {1,3,5} and {1,2,4}: again no member is contained in both. Adding the set {1} gives both pairs the meet {1}, and {1} is contained in every member, so it is also the least element. Every pair of members now has a meet and a join inside the family.
example.answer: Add {1} - the answer to GATE CSE 2004 Q.73, option (A).

gateAngle: Completeness questions are answered by listing the intersections (for meets) and unions (for joins) that the family is missing. On set-containment posets the join is the union and the meet the intersection, so the check is set arithmetic, not a diagram sweep.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2004 Q.73: which sets must be added to S to make it a complete lattice under containment? (A) {1} (B) {1}, {2,3} (C) {1}, {1,3} (D) {1}, {1,3}, {1,2,3,4}, {1,2,3,5}.
variations.why: The only missing meet is {1}; once it is added, every subset of the family has both a union and an intersection inside the family, so it is complete. Options C and D add sets that are not needed, and B adds a set that does not help.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Is the family {{2}, {2,3}, {2,4}, {2,3,4}} under set containment a complete lattice?
variations.answer: Yes. It is a lattice, and every finite lattice is complete.
variations.why: The meets are intersections: {2,3} n {2,4} = {2}, which is present. The joins are unions: {2,3} u {2,4} = {2,3,4}, which is present. So every pair has both bounds and the family is a 4-element lattice; finiteness makes it complete. This is the trap in the other direction - on a finite family, complete adds nothing.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Why is every finite lattice complete, while not every lattice is finite?
variations.answer: In a finite lattice, any subset is finite, and its join is the finite join of its elements, built two at a time by associativity; the empty subset is handled by the least and greatest elements.
variations.why: Completeness only adds power for infinite subsets, which is why the theory of complete lattices matters for infinite posets and not for the finite ones GATE draws.

trap.what: Treating 'complete lattice' as a stronger-sounding synonym for 'lattice' in a finite diagram, or forgetting the empty subset.
trap.why: For finite posets the two coincide, so the word 'complete' is a hint that the poset is a family of sets and the real question is whether it is closed under union and intersection.
trap.counterexample: The family {{1,2}, {1,2,3}, {1,3,5}, {1,2,4}, {1,2,3,4,5}} is not a lattice at all, because {1,3,5} and {1,2,4} have no meet in the family. Calling it an incomplete lattice would be the wrong diagnosis.

check.question: Is the divisor lattice of 12 complete?
check.answer: Yes - it is finite, so it is complete.
check.explanation: Every subset of the six divisors has an lcm and a gcd that are again divisors of 12, and the empty subset is handled by 1 and 12. Finiteness is the whole argument.
